Irena ignited the blood-and-oil fire through the gate, and the Mercy Below began tearing through Elias toward the storm drain as the crypt collapsed.
Irena must lead the surviving patients through the collapsing asylum to the old sea gate and toward a mainland rescue vessel after the storm weakens.
The aftermath must leave Elias's fate uncertain while preserving his confession as the surviving moral evidence of Saint Orison's crimes.

chapters.name: Beyond the Breakwater
chapters.content:
The fire did not burn like fire. It burned inward, a white seam beneath Elias’s skin, and wherever it passed the Mercy Below came apart in voices. The crypt shook around him. Water burst through the foundation stones in black columns, carrying fingers, teeth, and scraps of warden’s cloth toward the drain. Behind the iron gate, Irena shouted his name, but the sound arrived broken by the roar of the sea.

“Go!” Elias called.

His voice answered from his own mouth and from mouths opening along his ribs.

GO, they whispered.

The thing had found the shape of him again. His left hand lengthened, knuckles swelling into pale knobs; his face pulled sideways, and Mara looked out through one eye. Beneath his breastbone, the relic pulsed in the burning reliquary, trying to draw itself free.

Irena seized the gate with both hands. Water climbed around her ankles, carrying pages from the founder’s ledger and small, hair-lined bones.

“I am not leaving you.”

“You are leaving the living.”

Behind her, Tomas Bell clung to two patients. The others crowded the passage, soaked and white-faced. A crack split the ceiling. Stone fell between Elias and the gate.

Irena flinched but did not release it.

“Elias!”

The Mercy offered her his own face, young and unhurt, smiling through the falling dust.

“Come closer,” it said. “He is gone.”

“That isn’t him,” Irena said.

“No,” Elias answered, though the word emerged from three throats. “But it knows what I fear.”

The flood rose to his waist. He staggered toward the reliquary. Fire had blackened the stone, yet its lid remained open, glowing like a furnace beneath the water. Tendrils of altered flesh ran from his chest into the walls, searching for cracks and drains that led beyond the island.

It showed him a mainland chapel. A congregation knelt. Mara stood in the front pew, alive, singing her childhood hymn.

All you need do is open your hands.

For one terrible instant Elias wanted to believe. Then he remembered Mara’s actual hands, clenched in the blanket, reaching for him while he stood outside the locked room and listened to Bishop Haldane command him to continue.

“I will not use her again,” he said.

He drove his burning fingers into the relic.

The Mercy screamed. Elias’s spine arched. His bones became visible beneath his skin, not as a skeleton but as a second architecture trying to unfold. Wings, mouths, and grasping wrists crowded inside him. He seized the reliquary and dragged himself forward, leaving strips of flesh on the stones.

At the gate, Irena understood.

“Tomas, move!” she shouted. “Everyone to the sea passage!”

She forced the gate open far enough for the patients to crawl beneath it. Tomas went last, looking back until Irena shoved him through. Then she turned toward Elias.

He knelt before the reliquary. The Mercy covered his face. Only one eye remained his own.

“Seal it,” he told her.

“I can’t.”

“You can.”

The ceiling groaned. A wall folded inward, revealing seawater and the pale bodies of the transformed congregation. They swept toward the drain. One wore Agnes Vey’s six praying faces, each mouth pleading a different promise.

Irena lifted her rusted blade and struck the gate’s warped hinge. Once. Twice. On the third blow, it broke. The gate collapsed across the passage, pinning the Mercy’s reaching limbs beneath it.

Elias pulled the reliquary’s lid shut. The thing inside him tore at his throat, speaking in Mara’s voice, Saye’s voice, his own.

Forgive me, it said.

Elias pressed both hands against the lid.

“No.”

Not because forgiveness was impossible. Because the plea was not confession. It was escape.

He pushed until the stone sealed. Fire burst through the seams. The crypt vanished in steam, darkness, and the roar of the collapsing chapel.

Irena crawled through the sea passage with the others. The old gate opened beneath the cliff, where iron teeth grated against a boiling ocean. Behind them Saint Orison’s came down by sections: dormitory, tower, chapel. Windows flashed with faces, then disappeared beneath the surge. The bell rang once from somewhere below the water and fell silent.

They reached the breakwater at dawn.

The storm weakened so abruptly that the survivors stood in a strange, ringing quiet. Rain thinned to mist. Far offshore, a mainland rescue vessel appeared, its signal lamp trembling through the gray.

Only eleven survivors were found. There was no Rook, Vey, or Saye. Of Elias there was no body, only his prayer book, swollen with seawater, wedged beneath a slab of chapel stone. Irena kept it beneath her coat.

The official report named structural collapse, mass panic, and decades of concealed medical abuse. It described Saint Orison’s as an unsafe institution abandoned to the sea. No one recorded the crawling dead, the sixfold matron, or the black-white bone. The ocean had taken all evidence that could not be explained.

Weeks later, in a mainland infirmary, Irena opened the prayer book. The final page held Elias’s confession in a hand blurred by blood and salt. He had written what he did, what he heard, and why he obeyed. At the bottom there was no declaration of forgiveness. Only one sentence:

I will not call my fear a command again.

That night, as the survivors were moved inland, Irena heard a bell from the open sea.

She went to the breakwater. Rain drifted across the dark water. At its edge stood a figure with Elias’s face, coat hanging from his shoulders, hands folded as if in prayer.

She called once.

The figure turned. For an instant it was Elias. Then its features loosened, became rain, became black water sliding between the stones.

Or perhaps it knelt.

Far from Saint Orison’s, in a chapel whose doors were locked against the weather, a thin stream of seawater slipped beneath the altar. It gathered in the shape of a wing pierced by a nail, and somewhere below the floor, something answered with a bell.

set.name: Elias Vale
set.description: Elias is presumed dead or transformed beneath the collapsed, submerged chapel crypt. He forced the Mercy Below and the burning relic into the reliquary and sealed it with his own hands, but no body was recovered. His confession survives in his damaged prayer book; his tarnished crucifix and final physical fate are unknown. His last known goal was to prevent the entity from escaping through the storm drains without using sacrifice to purchase forgiveness.

set.name: Silas Rook
set.description: Rook is missing and presumed destroyed or buried in the collapsing asylum after transforming into official seals, teeth, and grasping hands. His pistol, commission, and bureaucratic flesh were left somewhere in Saint Orison's ruins. He remains an unresolved symbol of the institutional cover-up, with no confirmed surviving identity.

set.name: Mara Venn
set.description: Mara remains dead. The Mercy Below used her face and voice during Elias's final confrontation, but Elias refused to use the imitation again and no genuine fragment or resurrection was established. Her memory survives in Elias's confession and in the childhood hymn associated with her.

set.name: Dr. Lucien Saye
set.description: Saye is presumed dead or lost beneath the collapsing chapel treasury after holding back the transformed staff so Elias and Irena could obtain the consecrated oil. His notes enabled the destruction rite, but his body and survival remain unconfirmed.

set.name: Agnes Vey
set.description: Vey is missing and presumed drowned, buried, or still fused with the transformed staff after the asylum collapsed. Her six saintlike forms had served the Mercy Below and sought to deliver survivors to its promised salvation. No confirmed trace of her remains outside the sea-washed ruins.

set.name: Irena
set.description: Irena escaped Saint Orison's through the old sea gate with Tomas and the surviving patients, reaching the breakwater before a mainland rescue vessel arrived. She carries Elias's damaged prayer book and rusted blade, retains the altered seam on her arm, and knows his fate is uncertain. She remains emotionally burdened by his disappearance while guarding the truth preserved in his confession.
Irena led Tomas and the surviving patients through the old sea gate to the breakwater while Saint Orison's collapsed into the storm surge; eleven survivors were recovered at dawn.
Elias sealed the Mercy Below and the burning relic inside the collapsing reliquary, but no body was recovered from the crypt.
Irena recovered Elias's seawater-damaged prayer book beneath a chapel stone; its final page preserved his confession without declaring forgiveness.
A mainland rescue vessel recovered the survivors, while the official report attributed Saint Orison's destruction to structural collapse, mass panic, and concealed medical abuses.
Weeks later Irena heard a clapperless bell from the open sea and saw a figure with Elias's face dissolve into rain on the breakwater; black seawater then entered a distant chapel beneath an altar.
